title: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
summary: How a search engine analyzes text into terms, builds postings at any scale, answers Boolean and phrase queries, ranks with TF-IDF and cosine, finds the top k fast, and compresses it all in Lucene.
outcomes: Explain why an inverted index stores only the 1s of the term-document matrix and what the dictionary and postings hold
Build an inverted index by sort-based indexing, and explain how BSBI and SPIMI scale it past memory
Explain how an analyzer tokenizes and stems text, and why stemming raises recall but can cost precision
Trace the two-pointer postings merge, order AND terms by df, and explain when skip pointers help
Answer phrase and proximity queries with a positional index and estimate what positions cost in space
Compute TF-IDF and cosine scores for a small collection and explain why idf and length normalization change the ranking
Explain how MaxScore and WAND return the exact top k while fully scoring only a fraction of matching documents
Explain gap plus variable byte compression, immutable Lucene segments, refresh and deletes

lessons.title: From grep to the inverted index

blocks.md:
Suppose you want every document that mentions both *deploy* and *rollback*. The simplest method is a linear scan: read every document, every time, and check for the words. This is what `grep` does, and for a modest collection it is all you need: Shakespeare's collected works are a bit under one million words.

It stops working when the collection holds billions of words, when you want operators like *within 5 words of* (lesson 5 answers those), and when you want the **best** matches first instead of every match. The fix is to do the work once, ahead of time: build an **index**.

We will use one tiny collection through the whole course. Six documents, already lowercased:

- **d1**: the cache keeps the hot keys in the cache
- **d2**: the deploy broke the cache
- **d3**: roll back the deploy
- **d4**: the hot path skips the cache
- **d5**: a cache miss after the deploy
- **d6**: the miss rate fell after the roll back

A **token** is one occurrence of a word in the text, so *the* in d1 counts as three tokens. A **term** is an indexed unit, usually a normalized word: a token cleaned into one standard form, for example lowercased, so that every copy of the word maps to the same entry. These six documents contain 38 tokens and 17 distinct terms.

The most direct index is a **term-document incidence matrix**: one row per term, one column per document, and a 1 where the term occurs. A **Boolean query** combines terms with AND, OR and NOT and returns the set of documents that satisfy it. With the matrix, each operator becomes a bitwise operation on rows.

blocks.title: Term-document incidence matrix for six docs

scenes.caption: Each row is a term, each column a document. A 1 means the term occurs in that document. This is 7 terms of the 17 in the vocabulary.
Query deploy AND roll AND NOT cache. Pull the three rows: deploy is 011010, roll is 001001, cache is 110110.
NOT flips the cache row to 001001. Now every operator is a bitwise AND across the rows.
011010 AND 001001 AND 001001 = 001000: only d3 (roll back the deploy) matches.

blocks.prompt: Scale it up. A collection has 1 million documents of about 1000 words each, and 500,000 distinct terms. How many cells does the incidence matrix have, and at most how many of them can be 1?
blocks.reveal: The matrix has $500{,}000 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 5 \times 10^{11}$ cells, half a trillion. But each document has only about 1000 words, so there are at most $10^9$ ones. At least **99.8%** of the cells are zero. Storing the zeros is pure waste, which is the whole motivation for the next idea.

blocks.md:
An **inverted index** stores only the 1s. It has two parts:

- The **dictionary** (vocabulary): every distinct term once, plus statistics such as the **document frequency** $\mathrm{df}_t$, the number of documents that contain term $t$.
- For each term, a **postings list**: the docIDs of the documents containing it, sorted in increasing order. A **docID** is the integer that numbers a document, here 1 to 6 for d1 to d6. Each entry is a **posting**.

It is called inverted because it maps term to documents, the reverse of reading a document to find its terms.

blocks.title: Dictionary and postings for three terms

scenes.caption: The dictionary holds each distinct term once, with its document frequency (df): how many documents contain it.
Each term points to its postings list: the sorted docIDs of the documents that contain it. Only the 1s of the matrix are stored.
A query looks up each term in the dictionary and reads only those postings lists. Documents that contain neither term are never touched.
Intersecting 1, 2, 4, 5 with 5, 6 gives d5, the only document with both terms.

blocks.md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 6 and 7 add on top of the same postings.

blocks.question: Using the six documents, which documents match the Boolean query hot AND NOT deploy?
options: d1 and d4
d4 only
d1, d2, d4 and d5
No documents
blocks.explain: hot has postings d1, d4. deploy has postings d2, d3, d5, so NOT deploy is d1, d4, d6. The intersection is d1 and d4. Neither of them mentions deploy.

blocks.question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
blocks.explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 4). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

lessons.title: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings

blocks.md:
Index construction has four steps, as laid out in chapter 1 of the standard textbook, [Introduction to Information Retrieval by Manning, Raghavan and Schutze](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/a-first-take-at-building-an-inverted-index-1.html), which this course calls the textbook:

1. Collect the documents and give each a **docID**, a unique integer, usually assigned in order of arrival.
2. **Tokenize**: split text into tokens, for example `Friends, Romans, countrymen.` into `Friends`, `Romans`, `countrymen`.
3. **Normalize**: map tokens to terms, for example lowercase and stem to `friend`, `roman`, `countryman`. **Stemming** strips word endings by rule, such as a plural s, so *Romans* and *roman* become the same term. Lesson 3 takes these two steps apart in detail.
4. **Index**: record, for each term, the documents it occurs in.

The core of step 4 is **sort-based indexing**. Emit one (term, docID) pair per token, sort the pairs by term and then docID, merge repeated pairs from the same document, and split the result into a dictionary and postings lists. The watch below runs this on d1 to d3.

blocks.title: Sort-based indexing of d1 to d3

scenes.caption: Step 1: emit one (term, docID) pair per token, in document order. d1 to d3 produce 18 pairs.
Step 2: sort the pairs by term, then by docID. Equal terms are now adjacent and their docIDs are in increasing order.
Step 3: drop repeated (term, docID) pairs (greyed), keeping the count as the term frequency. 14 postings remain for 10 terms.
Step 4: each run of one term becomes a dictionary entry; its docIDs become the postings list. cache gets postings 1, 2 (df 2); the gets 1, 2, 3 (df 3).

blocks.md:
A posting can carry more than a docID. Most engines also store the **term frequency** $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$ (how many times $t$ occurs in $d$), which ranking needs. A **positional index** also stores the token positions, which phrase queries such as `"roll back"` need; lesson 5 builds one and answers phrases with it.

The dictionary is usually kept in memory and the much larger postings on disk. In memory, variable-length arrays beat linked lists on space and on cache-friendly scanning when updates are rare. The dictionary itself is a hash table or a search tree; a tree also answers prefix queries such as `depl*` (Lucene's .tip term index, lesson 9, is a compact prefix structure of this kind: an FST in Lucene 9, a trie since 10.3).

blocks.title: Building a tiny inverted index in Python

scenes.caption: Three documents, already lowercased. Real systems also strip punctuation and may stem words.
Tokenize and emit (term, docID) pairs in document order.
Sort: the core indexing step. Pairs for one term are now contiguous.
Group by term. Repeats inside one document increase a count instead of adding a posting.
Document frequency is just the length of each postings list.

blocks.prompt: Over all six documents, what is the document frequency of *the*, and what is its **collection frequency** (total occurrences across all documents)?
blocks.reveal: *the* is in every document, so $\mathrm{df} = 6$. Its counts per document are 3, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, so its collection frequency is **11**. The two statistics differ whenever a term repeats inside documents. Ranking will use df, because it measures how many documents a term can tell apart.

blocks.md: Sorting 18 pairs in memory is trivial. The textbook's model collection, **Reuters-RCV1** (about 800,000 Reuters news stories from 1996 and 1997), has about 100 million tokens. At 4 bytes each for a **termID** (an integer that stands for a term) and a docID, its pairs alone take 0.8 GB, and typical collections are one or two orders of magnitude larger. When the pairs do not fit in memory, index construction becomes an **external sort**: a sort that keeps most data on disk and must avoid random disk seeks, because sequential reads are far faster.

**Blocked sort-based indexing (BSBI)** does it in four steps: cut the collection into blocks of equal size, sort each block's termID-docID pairs in memory, write each sorted block (a **run**) to disk, then merge all runs at once. If 10 million pairs fit in memory, RCV1 becomes ten runs. The merge keeps a small read buffer per run and repeatedly takes the lowest termID with a priority queue, concatenating that term's postings from every run. Sorting dominates the complexity, $\Theta(T \log T)$ for $T$ pairs, but in practice parsing and the final merge dominate the time.

BSBI needs a term-to-termID map in memory, which for huge collections does not fit either. **Single-pass in-memory indexing (SPIMI)** drops termIDs: each block gets a fresh dictionary (a hash table) and every posting is appended straight to its term's list, which doubles in size when full. Only the block's terms are sorted, when the block is written, so the runs can still be merged in one linear pass.

blocks.title: Indexing a collection that does not fit in memory

scenes.caption: Parse the collection into pairs until a block that fits in memory is full: with 10 million pairs per block, Reuters-RCV1 gives 10 blocks.
BSBI sorts each block's termID-docID pairs in memory and writes the result to disk as a sorted run, an inverted index of that part of the collection.

The final merge opens all runs at once with a small read buffer each, picks the lowest termID left with a priority queue, and appends that term's postings from every run. Every disk read is sequential.
SPIMI keeps the same block, run and merge shape but changes the inside of a block: a hash dictionary of terms with growing postings lists, no termIDs and no sort of pairs.

blocks.md: For web-scale collections the textbook describes **distributed indexing** with MapReduce. Parser machines (the map phase) each take a split of the input, 16 or 64 MB, and write termID-docID pairs into one file per **term partition**, for example terms a to f, g to p and q to z. Inverter machines (the reduce phase) each collect one term partition from all parsers and sort it into postings lists. The result is a **term-partitioned** index; most large search engines prefer a **document-partitioned** index, where each machine holds a complete index of a subset of the documents. The segments of Lucene (the open-source search library that Elasticsearch and Solr are built on; lesson 9) are that second idea on one machine: every segment is a complete index of some documents.

Whatever normalization you apply at index time (lowercasing, stemming, stripping punctuation) you must apply identically to queries. If the index stores `cache` and the query parser passes `Cache` through unchanged, the dictionary lookup finds nothing.

**Stop words**, very common words such as *the* that carry little meaning on their own, can be dropped at index time to save space, but then a phrase made only of stop words, like *to be or not to be*, cannot be found. Lesson 6 shows that idf (inverse document frequency, a weight that falls as a term appears in more documents) gives such words near-zero weight anyway, which weakens the case for dropping them.

blocks.question: A team lowercases text when indexing but forgets to lowercase queries. A user searches for Deploy. What happens on our six documents?
options: It matches d2, d3 and d5 as expected
It matches every document, because the lookup falls back to a scan
It matches nothing, because the dictionary contains deploy but not Deploy
It matches only d3, the document that starts with roll
blocks.explain: The dictionary is an exact lookup structure. Index-time and query-time analysis must agree, or terms simply miss. Search libraries let you configure one analyzer (the chain of tokenize and normalize steps) and apply it on both sides for exactly this reason.

blocks.question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
blocks.explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

blocks.question: SPIMI can process bigger blocks than BSBI with the same amount of memory. Why?
options: SPIMI compresses the raw text before parsing it
SPIMI skips the final merge of the blocks
SPIMI only indexes terms that occur in more than one block
SPIMI appends each docID straight to its term's postings list, so it stores no termID per posting and never sorts an array of pairs
blocks.explain: BSBI holds (termID, docID) pairs and sorts them; SPIMI keeps one list per term in a hash table, so the term is stored once per list, not once per posting, and there is no pair array to sort. SPIMI still sorts the block's terms when writing it and still merges the runs at the end.

lessons.title: Analysis in depth: tokenizing, stemming and what normalizing costs

blocks.md:
A user searches `deployed` and d2 says *deploy*. Whether they meet is not decided by the index at all but by **analysis**: the steps that turn a stream of characters into terms, run identically on documents and on queries. Lesson 2 used the simplest analysis possible, lowercase and split on spaces. Real text breaks that quickly.

Three words first. A **token** is one occurrence of a character sequence in a document; a **type** is the class of all identical tokens; a **term** is a (usually normalized) type that goes into the dictionary. *to sleep perchance to dream* has 5 tokens and 4 types, and if *to* is dropped as a stop word, 3 terms.

**Tokenization** decides where tokens begin and end, and the textbook's hard cases show that every choice changes which queries match:

- Apostrophes: is *O'Neill* `neill`, `oneill`, `o'neill`, or `o` plus `neill`? Is *aren't* one token or `aren` plus `t`?
- Hyphens: *co-education* is one word, *Hewlett-Packard* joins two names, *San Francisco-Los Angeles* defeats both rules.
- Special tokens: `C++`, `C#`, `B-52`, email addresses, URLs, IP addresses and tracking numbers.
- Spaces inside one unit: *San Francisco*, *(800) 234-2333*, *Mar 11, 1983*.

There is no right answer in general, only consistency: whatever the tokenizer does to documents it must do to queries.

blocks.title: One sentence through three Lucene analyzers

nodes.label:
O'Neill's C++ co-education
talks aren't amusing

O'Neill's C++ co-education
talks aren't amusing

o'neill's c co education
talks aren't amusing

o'neil c co educ talk
aren't amus

scenes.caption: Real output from Lucene 9.11. The whitespace analyzer only splits on spaces: case, C++ and the hyphen survive, so a query for co education would miss.
StandardAnalyzer uses Unicode word-break rules and lowercases: C++ loses its plus signs (now c, which also matches C), the hyphen splits co-education, apostrophes inside words stay.
EnglishAnalyzer adds a possessive filter (drops 's), a 33-word stop list and the Porter stemmer: o'neil, educ, talk, amus. These terms are no longer words, only equivalence classes.

blocks.md: Other languages make tokenization harder. German writes compound nouns without spaces (*Lebensversicherungsgesellschaftsangestellter*, life insurance company employee), so German search benefits greatly from a **compound splitter** that checks whether a word divides into vocabulary words. Chinese, Japanese and Thai are written without spaces between words. One approach is **word segmentation** (longest vocabulary match, or a trained sequence model), which sometimes errs because several segmentations are possible. The other is to index short **character n-grams** regardless of word boundaries: a Chinese character usually carries meaning, and the most common word length is 2 characters.

After tokenizing, **normalization** maps tokens that differ superficially onto one term. The usual way is implicit **equivalence classes**: rules that delete characters, so *anti-discriminatory* and *antidiscriminatory* both become `antidiscriminatory`. The alternative is **query expansion**: keep tokens distinct and expand a query term into a list, such as *car* OR *automobile*. Expansion lists may be asymmetric: the textbook's query *windows* should match *Windows* (the operating system), but the query *window* should not. Too much classing hurts: deleting periods makes the query *C.A.T.* match every *cat*.

**Stemming** and **lemmatization** both reduce related forms of a word to one base form. Stemming is a crude rule set that chops off endings and often removes derivational suffixes too (*democracy*, *democratic*). Lemmatization uses a vocabulary and morphological analysis to return the dictionary form, the **lemma**: for *saw* a stemmer might return `s`, a lemmatizer `see` or `saw` depending on whether it is a verb or a noun.

The standard English stemmer is Martin Porter's 1980 algorithm: five phases of rules applied in order. Within a rule group the longest matching suffix wins (*caresses* to `caress` by SSES to SS, *ponies* to `poni` by IES to I). Later rules check the **measure** $m$ of the remaining stem, roughly its number of vowel-consonant sequences: (m>1) EMENT to nothing turns *replacement* into `replac` but leaves *cement* alone.

blocks.title: Porter's phases peeling suffixes

scenes.caption: Complex suffixes come off bit by bit, the example from Porter's own description: step 1 removes the plural, step 2 maps IZATION to IZE, step 3 ALIZE to AL, step 4 removes AL.
relational becomes relate in step 2. Step 4 would remove ATE only if the stem rel had measure above 1; it does not, so step 5a removes just the final E.
Lucene 9.11's PorterStemFilter: deployed loses ED and then step 1c turns the final Y into I, giving deploi. deployment loses MENT in step 4 and stays deploy. The two never meet.

blocks.prompt: Porter (as run by Lucene) maps *universe*, *university* and *universal* to one stem, and *news* to the same stem as *new*. It maps *deployed* to `deploi` but *deployment* to `deploy`. Name the two kinds of error.
blocks.reveal: **Over-stemming**: unrelated words collapse into one class (`univers`, `new`), so a query for *university* also retrieves documents about the universe. **Under-stemming**: related words land in different classes (`deploi` vs `deploy`), so a query for *deployed* misses documents that only say *deployment*. All outputs above are real Lucene 9.11 output. The exact stem string never matters, only which words share it. The lesson's opening query does work: *deployed* and d2's *deploy* both become `deploi`.

blocks.md: So does stemming help? The textbook's answer is: not much in aggregate for English. **Stemming increases recall while harming precision.** Recall is the share of all relevant documents that a query returns; precision is the share of returned documents that are relevant. Porter maps *operate*, *operating*, *operates*, *operation*, *operative*, *operatives* and *operational* all to `oper`, so the queries *operational research*, *operating system* and *operative dentistry* each start matching documents about the others. A lemmatizer would not fully fix this, because particular inflected forms belong to particular phrases. Languages with richer morphology are different: in the European CLEF (Cross-Language Evaluation Forum) evaluations, stemmers gave large gains for languages such as Spanish, German and Finnish, plus compound splitting for German.

In Lucene and Elasticsearch all of this is configured as an **analyzer**: zero or more **character filters** (rewrite the raw characters, for example strip HTML tags), exactly one **tokenizer** (split into tokens and record each token's position and character offsets), then zero or more **token filters** applied in order (lowercase, stop, stemming, synonyms). Lucene's EnglishAnalyzer, for example, is StandardTokenizer, then an English possessive filter, lowercase, a stop filter with 33 words such as *the*, *a* and *in*, and the Porter stem filter. Run it on four of our six documents and the index stores very different terms from lesson 2:

Analyzer en = new EnglishAnalyzer();
// tokenStream("body", text): print term@position for each token

   cach@1 keep@2 hot@4 kei@5 cach@8
d2 the deploy broke the cache
   deploi@1 broke@2 cach@4
d5 a cache miss after the deploy

d6 the miss rate fell after the roll back

blocks.caption: Real output of Lucene 9.11 EnglishAnalyzer (positions count from 0). Stop words vanish but leave gaps in the positions, so cach and keep in d1 are still known to be adjacent and hot is two places later.

blocks.md: Index-time and query-time analysis must match, a point lesson 2 made for lowercasing. Elasticsearch lets a field set a separate `search_analyzer`; if it stems documents but not queries, *deploy* becomes `deploi` in the index and the query term `deploy` finds nothing. Change an analyzer and you must reindex.

Analysis decides what a term is. Tokenizing and normalizing more aggressively makes more forms meet (recall) and more unrelated words collide (precision). Pick per language and domain, and apply the same chain to documents and queries.

blocks.question: Index and queries both go through lowercase, split on spaces, then Porter. Which query word matches d6 (*the miss rate fell after the roll back*) only because of stemming?
options: falls, because Porter maps both fell and falls to fall
hotter, because Porter strips the comparative ending
rates, because Porter maps rates to rate
skipped, because Porter maps it to a stem that d6 contains
blocks.explain: Lucene's Porter filter gives rates to rate, which d6 contains. falls becomes fall but fell stays fell: an irregular verb needs a lemmatizer. hotter stays hotter, and skipped becomes skip, which d6 does not contain. missing (to miss) and rolled (to roll) would also match d6 after stemming.

blocks.question: With Porter stemming, operate, operating, operational and operative all become oper. What happens to the Boolean query operating AND system?
options: It also matches documents about, say, operational research that mention a system, so recall rises and precision can fall
Nothing changes, because stemming is applied only at index time
It matches fewer documents, because stems are shorter than words
Precision rises, because one stem is more specific than four words
blocks.explain: Every form now shares one postings list, so the query matches any document with any of the forms plus system: more of the relevant documents (recall) but also documents about operative procedures or operational plans (precision loss). This is the textbook's example of why stemming barely helps English in aggregate.

lessons.title: Answering AND queries by merging postings

blocks.md:
Take a larger collection where *server* occurs in documents 2, 5, 9, 14, 21, 30, 38, 47 and *crash* in 5, 21, 40, 47. To answer `server AND crash`, look up both terms in the dictionary, fetch both postings lists and **intersect** them.

Because both lists are sorted, keep one pointer in each list; the figure calls them p1 and p2. Compare the two docIDs: if they are equal, output it and advance both; otherwise advance the pointer at the smaller docID, since that document cannot be in the other list.

blocks.title: Intersecting two postings lists with two pointers

scenes.caption: Two sorted postings lists. One pointer starts at the head of each. The answer list is empty.
Compare 2 with 5: 2 is smaller, so no document below 5 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 5 with 5: equal, so 5 goes into the answer and both pointers advance.
Compare 9 with 21: 9 is smaller, so no document below 21 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 14 with 21: 14 is smaller, so no document below 21 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 21 with 21: equal, so 21 goes into the answer and both pointers advance.
Compare 30 with 40: 30 is smaller, so no document below 40 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 38 with 40: 38 is smaller, so no document below 40 can be in both lists. Advance p1.
Compare 47 with 40: 40 is smaller, so advance p2.
Compare 47 with 47: equal, so 47 goes into the answer and both pointers advance. p2 has run off its list, so we stop: 9 comparisons in total, at most len(p1) + len(p2) = 12.

blocks.caption: Here p1 and p2 are the two postings lists, and x and y are their lengths. Each comparison advances at least one pointer, so the merge does at most x + y steps.

blocks.md:
This only works because every postings list uses the same global order. OR (union) and AND NOT are merges in the same style.

For an AND of many terms, order matters. The standard heuristic is to process terms in **increasing df**: start with the two shortest lists, and every intermediate result is then no longer than the shortest list. The dictionary already holds df, so the engine can plan the order before reading any postings from disk.

blocks.prompt: A query is `kernel AND server AND crash` with df 200, 8 and 4. In what order should the lists be intersected?
blocks.reveal: Start with **crash (4) and server (8)**: their intersection has at most 4 documents (here 3: 5, 21, 47). Then check those few candidates against kernel's 200 postings. Starting with kernel AND server would first walk up to 208 entries to build an intermediate result that can still be no larger than 8.

blocks.md:
When one list is much shorter than the other, even $O(x+y)$ wastes time walking the long list. **Skip pointers** add shortcuts at index time: some postings also store the position of a posting further ahead. If the skip target is still no larger than the docID we are looking for, we jump. A simple heuristic that works well in practice: for a list of length $P$, use $\sqrt{P}$ evenly spaced skips.

Here is where the square root comes from. With a skip every $s$ postings, reaching a target takes at most about $P/s$ jumps plus $s$ single steps inside the last stretch. More skips mean more jumps to check and store; fewer skips mean long stretches walked one by one. The sum $P/s + s$ is smallest when $s = \sqrt{P}$, about twice $\sqrt{P}$ steps instead of $P$: for the 16-entry list below, a skip every 4 postings.

blocks.title: Skip pointers on a 16-entry postings list

scenes.caption: A 16-entry list uses skip spacing sqrt(16) = 4: every 4th entry also stores where to jump (2 to 15, 15 to 34, 34 to 58). 58 has no entry 4 ahead, so only 3 skips exist.
Without skips, intersecting with the one-entry list [47] walks p1 through 2, 4, 7, ..., 40 before reaching 47: 11 entries visited.
With skips: p1 is at 2 and 2 < 47. Its skip target 15 is still at most 47, so jump to 15 instead of stepping through 4, 7, 11.
15 has a skip to 34, and 34 is at most 47: jump again. 34 skips to 58, which is past 47, so that skip is not taken.
Step normally from 34 to 40 to 47: match. p1 landed on 5 entries (2, 15, 34, 40, 47) instead of 11, at the cost of storing and checking skip pointers.

blocks.md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.
Intersection is a linear merge over sorted lists. Make it cheap by starting from the rarest term, and make long lists skippable.

blocks.question: You intersect a 10-entry list with a 1,000,000-entry list using the plain two-pointer merge. Roughly how many steps can it take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because the result has at most 10 documents
About 20, because each short entry costs two comparisons
About 1,000,000, because the pointer may have to walk the long list nearly to its end
About log2(1,000,000) = 20 per entry, because the lists are sorted
blocks.explain: The plain merge advances one step at a time, so in the worst case it walks the whole long list: O(x + y). Doing about 20 steps per short entry is what you get only if you add skips or binary search into the long list, which the plain merge does not do.

blocks.question: Why does the engine keep df in the in-memory dictionary even for a pure Boolean search engine?
options: Boolean retrieval multiplies scores by df
It lets the planner order terms by list length before reading any postings
The merge algorithm needs df to know when to stop
It is needed to decompress postings
blocks.explain: Knowing each list's length up front lets the query optimizer intersect the shortest lists first. The merge itself stops when either pointer runs off its list, so it never needs df.

lessons.title: Phrase and proximity queries with a positional index

blocks.md: Search for the phrase `"deploy cache"`. The AND merge of lesson 4 returns d2 and d5, because both contain both words. Neither contains the phrase: d2 says *deploy broke the cache* and d5 says *cache miss after the deploy*. A docID-only index cannot tell the difference, because it threw word order away when it recorded only which documents contain a term. Lesson 1 promised operators such as *within 5 words of*; they need the same missing information.

The first fix is a **biword index**: treat every pair of consecutive words as one vocabulary term. d3 *roll back the deploy* yields `roll back`, `back the` and `the deploy`. Two-word phrases become a single lookup. Longer phrases are split into overlapping biwords joined by AND: *stanford university palo alto* becomes `stanford university` AND `university palo` AND `palo alto`, which can return **false positives**, documents that contain all three pairs but never the four words in a row. Biwords also inflate the vocabulary. Our 6 documents have 17 terms but 24 distinct biwords; in our run, the 1,400 abstracts of the Cranfield collection (lesson 6 tells its history), after Lucene's EnglishAnalyzer (lesson 3) stemmed them and dropped stop words, had 5,171 terms and 80,462 distinct biwords, 15.6 times as many. And single-word queries still need an ordinary index.

The standard fix is a **positional index**: each posting becomes docID: tf: ⟨positions⟩, where a position is the token's index in the document (here counted from 1; Lucene counts from 0). The tf is just the number of positions. For our documents:

- **the**: d1 ⟨1, 4, 8⟩; d2 ⟨1, 4⟩; d3 ⟨3⟩; d4 ⟨1, 5⟩; d5 ⟨5⟩; d6 ⟨1, 6⟩
- **cache**: d1 ⟨2, 9⟩; d2 ⟨5⟩; d4 ⟨6⟩; d5 ⟨2⟩
- **deploy**: d2 ⟨2⟩; d3 ⟨4⟩; d5 ⟨6⟩
- **hot**: d1 ⟨5⟩; d4 ⟨2⟩

To answer a phrase, merge on docID exactly as before, starting from the rarest term. For each document both terms share, walk their two position lists with two pointers and report the places where the second term sits exactly one position after the first.

blocks.title: Matching the phrase "the cache" with positions

scenes.caption: The docID merge already ran: the and cache are both in d1, d2, d4 and d5, so the AND query returns all four. Now check positions inside each candidate, starting with d1.
the at 1, cache at 2: 2 minus 1 is 1, so they are adjacent. Record a match (written doc:position of the) and advance both pointers.
the at 4, cache at 9: the gap is 5, so cache is too far ahead. The pointer on the must catch up: advance p1.
the at 8, cache at 9: adjacent again, a second match in d1. Both lists are now used up.
In d5 the is at 5 and cache at 2: cache comes first, so advance p2, and its list ends. d5 has both words but not the phrase.
The same check finds the cache at 4 to 5 in d2 and 5 to 6 in d4. The phrase matches d1, d2 and d4; the AND query had also returned d5.

blocks.md: A **proximity query** uses the same walk with a looser test. In the textbook's example from Westlaw, a commercial legal search service, `employment /3 place`, the operator /k means within $k$ words on either side, so the check becomes $|pos_2 - pos_1| \le k$ instead of $pos_2 - pos_1 = 1$. A biword index cannot answer such queries at all. Here is the whole algorithm on the six documents, with its real output:

blocks.code:
def positional_and(t1, t2, k=None):
    """phrase "t1 t2" when k is None, else t1 /k t2"""
    p1, p2 = sorted(pos[t1].items()), sorted(pos[t2].items())
    i = j = 0; out = []
    while i < len(p1) and j < len(p2):
        (d1, l1), (d2, l2) = p1[i], p2[j]
        if d1 == d2:                      # same doc: compare positions
            for a in l1:
                for b in l2:
                    if (b - a == 1) if k is None else abs(b - a) <= k:
                        out.append((d1, a, b))
            i += 1; j += 1
        elif d1 < d2: i += 1
        else: j += 1
    return out

positional_and("the", "cache")    # [(1,1,2), (1,8,9), (2,4,5), (4,5,6)]
positional_and("roll", "back")    # [(3,1,2), (6,7,8)]
positional_and("deploy", "cache") # []
positional_and("hot", "cache", 3) # [(1,5,2)]
blocks.caption: pos maps term to {docID: [positions]}. The nested loop is the simple version; the textbook's Figure 2.12 keeps a sliding window so each position is visited a bounded number of times. Outputs are from running it.

blocks.prompt: Now the query `deploy /3 cache`. The AND query returns d2 and d5. Which of them match within 3 words, and what changes with /4?
blocks.reveal: Only **d2**: deploy at 2, cache at 5, distance 3. In d5 cache is at 2 and deploy at 6, distance 4, so d5 joins only at `deploy /4 cache`. Proximity is symmetric (either order), unlike a phrase: the phrase `"deploy cache"` matches neither document.

blocks.md: Positions are not free. The textbook notes that a Boolean query's cost is now bounded by the number of tokens $T$ rather than the number of documents, and gives rules of thumb: a positional index is **2 to 4 times** as large as a non-positional one, and a compressed positional index is about **one third to one half** of the raw text. We measured Cranfield after EnglishAnalyzer (gap plus variable byte coding, lesson 9): docIDs and tf take 197,996 bytes, positions add 185,577, a ratio of 1.94, and the total is 0.25 of the 1.55 MB text, both under the rule of thumb because these abstracts are short (about 111 indexed tokens each) and stop words were removed. In the same run Lucene 9.11 wrote 135,014 bytes of .doc (docIDs, frequencies and skip data) and 176,060 of .pos.

Real systems combine the two ideas. Common phrases go into a phrase or biword index and everything else uses positions. The best phrases to precompute are those whose words are common but whose phrase is rare: the textbook estimates a biword entry speeds up *Britney Spears* by about 3 times but *The Who* by about 1000 times. Williams et al. (2004) added a **next word index** (for each term, the terms that follow it) and answered a typical mix of web phrase queries in a quarter of the time of a positional index alone, for 26% more space.

In Elasticsearch, [`match_phrase`](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl-match-query-phrase.html) analyzes the text and builds a phrase query that reads Lucene's .pos file. Its `slop` is the number of positions allowed between matching tokens, default 0; transposed terms need a slop of 2.

A positional index stores, for each term and document, the list of positions. A phrase or proximity query merges on docID first and then compares positions inside each shared document, so it costs work per occurrence, not just per document.

Dropping stop words at index time breaks phrases made of them (*to be or not to be*, *The Who*). Lucene keeps a gap in the positions where a stop word was removed, so distances stay right, but the stop word itself can no longer be matched.

blocks.question: Using the positional index above, which documents match the phrase "the cache", and which match hot /3 cache?
options: "the cache": d1, d2, d4 and d5; hot /3 cache: d1 and d4
"the cache": d1 only; hot /3 cache: d1 and d4
"the cache": d1, d2 and d4; hot /3 cache: d1 and d4
"the cache": d1, d2 and d4; hot /3 cache: d1 only
blocks.explain: d5 has the at 5 and cache at 2, not adjacent, so the phrase matches d1, d2 and d4. For hot /3 cache, d1 has hot at 5 and cache at 2 (distance 3, a match) while d4 has hot at 2 and cache at 6 (distance 4, too far).

blocks.question: Why can a phrase query on a positional index not finish in O(x + y) steps, where x and y are the two terms' document frequencies, even with skip pointers?
options: For each document both terms share, it must also walk both position lists, so the work grows with the number of occurrences, not documents
Positions break the docID sort order, so the docID merge no longer works
A phrase query must scan every document in the collection
Skip pointers cannot be stored in a positional index
blocks.explain: The docID merge (with skips) still works exactly as in lesson 4. The extra cost is inside each shared document: comparing positions costs time proportional to how often the two terms occur there. That is why the textbook bounds positional queries by the token count T instead of the document count N.

lessons.title: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity

blocks.md:
Boolean queries return sets. Most users type a **free text query** (a few words, no operators) and expect the best documents first. So we score each document.

Start with the **bag of words** view: a document is just the counts of its terms, ignoring order. *Mary is quicker than John* and *John is quicker than Mary* are the same bag. The count of term $t$ in document $d$ is its **term frequency** $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$.

The simplest score is the **overlap score**: add up, over the query terms, how many times each occurs in the document. Run it on our six documents for the query `the cache miss`. The user clearly cares about cache misses, and only d5 says *cache miss*.

blocks.prompt: With the overlap score (sum of tf over the, cache, miss), which document ranks first?
blocks.reveal: **d1**, with 5: three copies of *the* and two of *cache*. d5 scores 3 and ties with d2, d4 and d6. Raw counts treat every term as equally important, so the most common word in English does most of the scoring.

blocks.md: We need to discount terms that appear everywhere. One option is collection frequency, but document frequency works better for telling documents apart. In a collection of Reuters news stories that the textbook uses, *try* and *insurance* occur about equally often in total (10,422 and 10,440 times), yet *try* is spread over 8,760 documents and *insurance* over only 3,997. A query on *insurance* should reward its documents more. The **inverse document frequency** of a term, for a collection of $N$ documents, is:

blocks.caption: A term in every document gets log(1) = 0. The rarer the term, the higher its idf.

blocks.md: Where does this come from? $\mathrm{df}_t/N$ is the chance that a randomly picked document contains $t$, so $N/\mathrm{df}_t$ says how many documents you go through, on average, to meet one that contains it. The log of that ratio equals $-\log(\mathrm{df}_t/N)$, which grows as the term gets more surprising, and it compresses the range: a term in 1 of 1,000,000 documents gets 6 instead of 1,000,000. On our six documents, *cache* is in 4, so its idf is $\log_{10}(6/4) = 0.176$; *miss* is in 2, so $\log_{10} 3 = 0.477$; *the* is in all 6, so $\log_{10} 1 = 0$.

blocks.title: idf = log10(N/df) when N = 1,000,000

scenes.caption: A term in one document out of a million gets idf 6. Every factor of 10 more documents costs exactly 1 point (log base 10).

blocks.md: The idea is older than the formula. In 1972 Karen Sparck Jones argued that matches on rare, specific terms should count for more than matches on frequent ones, and weighted a term occurring in $n$ of $N$ documents by $f(N) - f(n) + 1$ with $f(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$. Here $f(n)$ is about the number of bits needed to write $n$, so the weight is roughly $\log_2(N/n) + 1$: the same log of a ratio as idf. Sparck Jones tested it on Cranfield, an early test collection of aeronautics paper abstracts with queries and known relevant answers, built at the College of Aeronautics in Cranfield, England. In Sparck Jones's 200-document Cranfield example a term in 90 documents got weight 2 and a term in 3 documents got weight 7.

**TF-IDF** (term frequency times inverse document frequency) combines the two signals: the weight of term $t$ in document $d$ is its count times its rarity. A document's score for a query is the sum of the weights of the query terms:

blocks.caption: Multiply each query term's count in the document by its idf, then add those products over the terms of the query q to get document d's score.

blocks.title: Query the cache miss: raw counts vs TF-IDF

scenes.caption: Overlap score: total occurrences of query terms. d1 wins with 5, mostly from three copies of the and two of cache. d5, the only doc about a cache miss, ties with four others at 3.
TF-IDF with log10 idf: the gets idf 0, cache 0.176, miss 0.477. d5 now ranks first (0.653), then d6 (0.477) and d1 (0.352).

blocks.md: Twenty occurrences are unlikely to be twenty times as significant as one. A common fix is **sublinear tf scaling**: use $\mathrm{wf}_{t,d} = 1 + \log \mathrm{tf}_{t,d}$ when $\mathrm{tf}_{t,d} > 0$ (and 0 otherwise) in place of raw tf. Other engines dampen tf differently: Lucene, the open-source search library that Elasticsearch and Solr are built on, used the square root of tf in its classic scoring.

blocks.title: Raw tf versus sublinear tf weights

x.label: occurrences of the term in the doc (tf)

scenes.caption: Raw tf is linear: the 10th occurrence counts as much as the 1st.
Sublinear scaling 1 + log10(tf): one occurrence gives 1, ten give 2, twenty give 2.3. Repetition still helps, but with fast diminishing returns.
Lucene's classic TF-IDF used sqrt(tf): ten occurrences give 3.16. All three agree at tf = 1; they differ in how much repetition is rewarded.

blocks.md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

blocks.question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
blocks.explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

blocks.question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
blocks.explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

lessons.title: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity

blocks.md:
The **vector space model** treats each document as a vector with one dimension per dictionary term (17 here, hundreds of thousands in practice) with its tf-idf weights as coordinates. A query is just a very short document, so it becomes a vector too. Ranking becomes: which document vectors point in nearly the same direction as the query?

Why direction and not raw overlap? Two documents with the same mix of terms can have very different raw weights just because one is longer. The standard fix is the **cosine similarity**: the dot product of the two vectors divided by the product of their Euclidean lengths.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{score}(q,d) = \frac{\vec V(q) \cdot \vec V(d)}{|\vec V(q)|\,|\vec V(d)|} = \frac{\sum_t w_{t,q}\, w_{t,d}}{\sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,q}^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,d}^2}}
blocks.caption: Multiply the query's and the document's weight for each term t and add up (the dot product), then divide by the two vector lengths. Dividing by the lengths turns both vectors into unit vectors, so the score is the cosine of the angle between them, between 0 and 1 for non-negative weights.

blocks.title: TF-IDF weights before and after length normalization

scenes.caption: Raw tf-idf weights (tf x log10(N/df)) for 6 of the 17 terms. The column for the is all zero because it is in every document. d1 has cache weight 0.35 because cache occurs twice.
Divide each row by its document's full vector length (over all 17 terms): d1 1.472, d2 0.853, d5 1.087. d1's cache weight drops to 0.24, close to d2's 0.21.

After normalization every row is a unit vector, so a document cannot win just by having more or heavier terms. d5 has the largest weight on miss (0.44), the rarest query term, plus a weight on cache, so it will score highest.

blocks.md: For the query `the cache miss` we use idf as each query term's weight: $(0, 0.176, 0.477)$ for (the, cache, miss). Its length is 0.509, so the unit query vector is $(0, 0.346, 0.938)$. The query leans heavily toward *miss*, the rarest of its terms.

blocks.prompt: With plain TF-IDF sums, d1 scored 0.352 and d2 scored 0.176: d1 was twice as good. What happens to that gap under cosine scoring?
blocks.reveal: It nearly closes: **d1 0.083 vs d2 0.071**. d1 has four other non-zero terms (keeps, keys and in with idf 0.778 each, plus hot with 0.477), so its vector length is 1.472 against d2's 0.853. Its two copies of *cache* are a smaller share of a longer vector.

blocks.title: Cosine scores for the query the cache miss

scenes.caption: Full cosine: dot product divided by the document length and the query length 0.509. d5 0.468, d6 0.307, d1 0.083. The rare term miss decides most of the ranking.

blocks.md: Computing a dot product against every document would be far too slow. Instead, walk the postings of the query terms only. **Term-at-a-time** scoring keeps one **accumulator** per candidate document and adds each term's contribution as its postings are read. Postings store the integer tf, not a float weight; idf is derived from df (or $N/\mathrm{df}$ stored at the head of the list) at query time. A heap then extracts the top $K$. The alternative, **document-at-a-time**, walks all query lists together in docID order and finishes one document before moving on. Lesson 8 shows why engines prefer it: walking in docID order lets them skip documents that cannot reach the top $K$.

blocks.title: Term-at-a-time scoring with accumulators
blocks.code:
import math
N = 6
index = {"cache": [(1, 2), (2, 1), (4, 1), (5, 1)],
         "miss":  [(5, 1), (6, 1)]}
length = {1: 1.472, 2: 0.853, 4: 1.212, 5: 1.087, 6: 1.457}
scores = {}                      # accumulators
for term in ["cache", "miss"]:   # "the" has idf 0: skip it
    postings = index[term]
    idf = math.log10(N / len(postings))
    for doc, tf in postings:
        # query weight idf times doc weight tf*idf
        scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0) + idf * tf * idf
for doc in scores:
    scores[doc] /= length[doc]
top = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:3]
print([(d, round(s, 3)) for d, s in top])

scenes.caption: Postings store (docID, tf). Document vector lengths are precomputed at index time, over all terms of each document.
First query term cache: df 4, so idf = log10(6/4) = 0.176.
Walk cache's postings, adding each document's contribution to its accumulator. d1 has tf 2, so it gets twice as much.
Second term miss: idf 0.477. Only d5 and d6 are touched; d5's accumulator grows to 0.259.
Divide by document length. The query's length is the same for every document, so skipping it does not change the ranking.
Keep the top K (here 3). Large engines use a heap rather than a full sort.

blocks.md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

Cosine ranking does not require a document to contain all query terms. d6 never mentions *cache* yet ranks second, above d1 which has *cache* twice, because *miss* carries most of the query's weight. If you need every term, combine scoring with a Boolean AND filter.

The textbook's SMART notation, named after Gerard Salton's SMART retrieval system at Cornell, names a scheme ddd.qqq: tf, df and normalization letters for documents, then for queries. Our worked example is **ntc.ntc**: natural (raw) tf, idf (t) and cosine (c) on documents, and on the query, whose tf is 1 per term. A standard alternative is **lnc.ltc**: log tf, no idf and cosine for documents; log tf, idf and cosine for queries.

blocks.prompt: Recompute d5 for the query the cache miss under lnc.ltc. Every word in d5 (*a cache miss after the deploy*) occurs once. Does the ranking change?
blocks.reveal: Each of d5's six terms has log tf weight $1 + \log_{10} 1 = 1$ and no idf, so after cosine normalization each is $1/\sqrt 6 = 0.408$. The unit query vector is still $(0, 0.346, 0.938)$, so d5 scores $0.408 \times (0.346 + 0.938) = 0.524$ instead of 0.468. Over all documents (computed): d5 0.524, d6 0.338, d1 0.161, d2 0.160, d4 0.145. The order survives, but d1 and d2 are now nearly tied: without idf on the document side, d1's rare words *keeps* and *keys* no longer inflate its length. The scheme is a choice that changes the numbers.

blocks.question: Using raw tf weights, you append a document to itself (every tf doubles, nothing else changes, and the document collection statistics stay the same). What happens to its cosine score for any query?
options: It doubles
It stays exactly the same
It increases by a factor of sqrt(2)
It drops, because the document is now longer
blocks.explain: With raw tf, every weight doubles, so the vector is scaled by 2. Scaling a vector does not change its direction, and cosine depends only on direction, so the score is unchanged. A plain TF-IDF sum would double, which is exactly the length bias cosine removes.

blocks.question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
blocks.explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

lessons.title: Getting the top k fast: tiers, MaxScore and WAND

blocks.md: The accumulator loop of lesson 7 reads every posting of every query term and keeps a score for every document that matches any term. On six documents that is nothing. On a web collection where one query term has a df of 10 million, a two-word query reads more than 10 million postings to show 10 results. Engines avoid that in two ways: **inexact** methods that only score likely winners and may miss a true top-$k$ document, and **safe** methods that return exactly the top $k$ while skipping documents that provably cannot make it.

The textbook's inexact heuristics:

- **Index elimination**: only traverse terms whose idf exceeds a threshold (for *catcher in the rye*, only *catcher* and *rye*), or only score documents containing many or all query terms.
- **Champion lists**: at index time keep, per term, the $r$ documents with the highest weight; at query time score only the union of the query terms' champion lists, with $r$ well above $K$.
- **Static quality** $g(d)$, a query-independent score such as review counts, added to the cosine, with postings ordered by $g(d)$ so good documents are met first.
- **Impact ordering**: sort each postings list by decreasing tf, stop after a prefix, and process terms in decreasing idf order.

blocks.title: A tiered index falls back only when it must

scenes.caption: The textbook's example splits each term's postings by tf into tiers: tier 1 holds postings with tf above 20, tier 2 above 10, tier 3 the rest. Within a tier postings stay in docID order.
A query first runs against tier 1 only. If that yields at least K documents, the answer comes from a small slice of the index.
If tier 1 yields fewer than K documents, processing falls back to tier 2, then tier 3. This fixes the main danger of champion lists and index elimination: ending with too few results.

blocks.md: Inexact methods can drop a document that exhaustive scoring would rank in the top k, because the selection (champion lists, tiers, idf thresholds) is fixed before the query arrives. The textbook argues this is often acceptable, since cosine is itself only a proxy for relevance, but it is a quality trade, not a free speedup.

The safe methods work **document-at-a-time** (DAAT): one cursor per query term, all moving through their postings in docID order, and each document is fully scored when the cursors reach it. A min-heap of size $k$ holds the best documents so far; once it is full, its smallest score is the **threshold** $\theta$, and a new document enters only with a score above $\theta$. Each term also has an **upper bound** $UB_t$: a number no smaller than the largest score the term contributes to any document, either recorded at index time or derived from the scoring formula. BM25, the scoring function Lucene uses by default (lesson 9 introduces it), has a ceiling on every term's contribution, so Lucene can derive the bound without storing it.

blocks.tex: \text{score}(d) \le \sum_{t \in q,\; d \in \text{postings}(t)} UB_t \qquad\text{so if}\qquad \sum_{t \ni d} UB_t \le \theta,\ \text{skip } d
blocks.caption: A document can only beat the threshold if the upper bounds of the terms it contains add up to more than theta. Skipped documents are never scored, and the top k cannot change.

blocks.md: **MaxScore** (Turtle and Flood, 1995) sorts the terms by upper bound. The longest group of low-bound terms whose bounds sum to at most $\theta$ is **non-essential**: a document containing only those terms cannot win. Only the remaining **essential** terms produce candidates; non-essential lists are just probed, by skipping to each candidate. As $\theta$ rises, more terms become non-essential. **WAND** (Weak AND, Broder et al., 2003) is finer grained. Sort the cursors by their current docID and add up their bounds in that order; the first cursor where the sum exceeds $\theta$ gives the **pivot** document. No document before the pivot can win, so the cursors behind it jump straight to the pivot using skip data (lesson 4). If all cursors up to the pivot already sit on it, score it fully.

blocks.title: WAND skipping postings: bounds 0.2, 0.5, 1.4

scenes.caption: Three query terms; cells are docIDs. We want the top 1, and the best document so far scores 0.8, so theta = 0.8. Cursors start at 1, 2 and 5.
In docID order: A at 1 (sum 0.2), B at 2 (sum 0.7), C at 5 (sum 2.1 > 0.8). Pivot is doc 5. Any earlier doc has at most A + B = 0.7, so B jumps to 7 and A to 6.
C now sits first, on the pivot: score doc 5 fully. Only C contains it, 0.6, not above 0.8, so it is rejected. C advances to 10.
A at 6 (0.2), B at 7 (0.7), C at 10 (2.1): pivot is doc 10. B and A jump to 10, skipping 6, 7 and 8 without scoring them.
All three sit on doc 10: score it, 0.1 + 0.4 + 1.2 = 1.7 > 0.8. It becomes the best document and theta rises to 1.7. The cursors move to 12, 13 and 14.
Pivot is doc 14 (0.2 + 0.5 + 1.4 = 2.1 > 1.7), so B jumps past 14 and its list ends. Now A + C = 1.6, not above 1.7: no pivot, stop. Of 11 matching docs, 2 were scored.

blocks.prompt: Same three lists and the same starting theta = 0.8, but with MaxScore. Which terms are essential, and which documents become candidates?
blocks.reveal: Sorted by bound: A 0.2, B 0.5, C 1.4. A + B = 0.7 is at most 0.8, so **A and B are non-essential** and only **C** is essential: the candidates are C's documents 5, 10 and 14, never 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12 or 13. For doc 5, C gives 0.6; 0.6 + 0.7 could still beat 0.8, so B is probed (it skips to 7: no match); 0.6 + 0.2 cannot, so A is never touched. Doc 10 scores 1.7 and theta rises; doc 14 gives 0.3, and 0.3 + 0.7 is below 1.7, so it is dropped after one lookup.

blocks.md: Does this hold up on real data? We ran it on the Cranfield collection (1,400 aeronautics abstracts, 225 queries of 11.4 terms on average after Lucene's EnglishAnalyzer) with BM25 scoring. First we checked our Python BM25 against Lucene 9.11 itself: identical top-10 documents in identical order for all 225 queries, largest score difference 2.4e-6 (float rounding). Matching Lucene needed one detail: it stores each document length in one byte, so doc 51's 124 tokens are scored as 120. Then for top 10, exhaustive term-at-a-time scoring touched 968.7 documents per query; MaxScore scored 501.4 candidates (some only partly, dropped once their bound fell short) and WAND fully scored 151.5, and both returned exactly the exhaustive top-10 scores on 225 of 225 queries. For top 100 the savings shrink, because the threshold stays lower: MaxScore 735.6, WAND 501.0.

blocks.title: Documents scored per Cranfield query (BM25)

scenes.caption: Top 10, averaged over 225 queries: same results, from 968.7 scored documents down to 501.4 (MaxScore) and 151.5 (WAND). Measured in Python, so we count work rather than time.
Top 100: the 100th best score is lower, so fewer documents can be ruled out. MaxScore scores 735.6 and WAND 501.0 per query.

blocks.code:
def wand(cursors, k):                  # one cursor per query term
    heap = []                            # min-heap of (score, doc)
    while True:
        theta = heap[0][0] if len(heap) == k else 0.0
        cursors.sort(key=lambda c: c.doc())
        acc, pivot = 0.0, None
        for i, c in enumerate(cursors):
            if c.doc() == INF: break
            acc += c.ub                  # upper bound of this term
            if acc > theta: pivot = i; break
        if pivot is None: return heap    # nothing left can win
        pd = cursors[pivot].doc()
        if cursors[0].doc() == pd:       # every cursor before pivot is on pd
            s = sum(c.score() for c in cursors if c.doc() == pd)
            for c in cursors:
                if c.doc() == pd: c.next()
            push_top_k(heap, k, pd, s)
        else:                            # jump a lagging cursor to pd
            lag = [c for c in cursors[:pivot] if c.doc() < pd]
            max(lag, key=lambda c: c.ub).advance(pd)
blocks.caption: The WAND loop from our Cranfield run (cursor class and heap push omitted). advance(pd) uses the skip data to land on the first posting at or after pd.

blocks.md: Lucene took this path in steps. After it switched its default to BM25, whose scores are naturally bounded, it implemented WAND for top-k disjunctions ([LUCENE-4100](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/LUCENE-4100)); its benchmarks showed disjunctions 40% to 13 times faster. It then adopted **block-max WAND** (Ding and Suel, 2011): keep a maximum separately for each fixed-size block of postings, so one outlier document no longer loosens the bound for a whole list. Lucene stores each block's competitive (term frequency, document length) pairs rather than scores and derives the block maximum from them, so the similarity can still change at search time. Term queries became 3 to 7 times faster and disjunctions between 8% slower and 15 times faster. It shipped in Lucene 8.0 and Elasticsearch 7.0. The price: skipped documents are never counted, so the total hit count is only exact up to a limit (`track_total_hits` in Elasticsearch), and scores may no longer be negative, so matching one more term can only raise a score.

Safe top-k pruning keeps a running threshold, the k-th best score so far, and a score upper bound per term (or per block). Any document whose bounds cannot beat the threshold is skipped with the skip data, so the top k is exactly what exhaustive scoring would return.

blocks.question: WAND and champion lists both avoid scoring most matching documents. Why does WAND always return the same top k as exhaustive scoring, while champion lists may not?
options: WAND scores more documents in total, so it is slower but exact
Champion lists use a different scoring function from WAND
WAND skips a document only when the bounds of its terms cannot beat the current k-th best score; champion lists drop documents chosen before the query is known
WAND only works for single-term queries, where exactness is easy
blocks.explain: WAND's skip test is a proof: an upper bound on the document's score is at most the threshold, so it cannot enter the top k. Champion lists keep the top r documents per term chosen at index time; a document that is moderate on several query terms can rank first overall yet sit in no champion list.

blocks.question: Three query terms have upper bounds 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0. The heap is full and theta = 1.2. Which documents can be skipped without scoring?
options: Only documents that contain none of the three terms
Every document that lacks either the 1.0 term or the 0.6 term
Documents whose actual score is below 1.2, which must be computed first
Documents containing only the 0.3 and 0.6 terms (bound 0.9), but not documents containing the 0.3 and 1.0 terms (bound 1.3)
blocks.explain: A document can be skipped when the bounds of the terms it contains sum to at most theta. 0.3 + 0.6 = 0.9 cannot beat 1.2, so such documents are skipped. 0.3 + 1.0 = 1.3 could, so a document lacking only the 0.6 term must still be scored. Skipping by actual score would require scoring first, which is the work we wanted to avoid.

lessons.title: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene

blocks.md:
Postings dominate index size. The Reuters-RCV1 collection (Reuters Corpus Volume 1, introduced in lesson 2) used in the textbook has 800,000 documents and 100,000,000 postings (docIDs only). A docID needs $\log_2 800{,}000 \approx 20$ bits, so the uncompressed postings take $10^8 \times 20 / 8 = 250$ MB.

The trick is that postings are sorted, so we can store **gaps** between consecutive docIDs. A frequent term appears in many nearby documents, so its gaps are small numbers that need far fewer bits.

blocks.title: Gap encoding plus variable byte codes

scenes.caption: A postings list of 5 docIDs. Stored as fixed 32-bit integers it takes 20 bytes.
Store the first docID, then only the gap to the previous one. Gaps are small when a term is frequent, because its documents are close together.
Variable byte: 7 payload bits per byte, with the high bit set on the last byte of each number. Gaps below 128 take 1 byte; 19869 needs 3. Total 7 bytes instead of 20.

blocks.md:
**Variable byte (VB)** encoding writes each gap in as few whole bytes as possible: 7 payload bits per byte, with the first bit as a continuation flag set on the last byte of a number. The textbook reports that VB shrinks the Reuters-RCV1 postings to 116 MB, more than a 50% saving. Byte-aligned codes decode fast; bit-level codes such as gamma codes compress further at the cost of more bit manipulation. A **gamma code** writes a number's binary digits without the leading 1, preceded by how many there are in unary, that many 1s and then a 0: 13 is 1101 in binary, so the offset is 101, its length 3 is written 1110, and the code is 1110101.

Lucene's 9.9 postings format goes a step further: docIDs and frequencies are delta-encoded (stored as gaps) and packed into blocks of 128 integers that share one bit width, with leftover entries written as variable-length ints, and with skip data per block. Lucene 10.4's format (Lucene104PostingsFormat, still current in 10.6) doubled the block to 256 integers.

blocks.prompt: Which postings list compresses better with gap encoding: the one for *the*, or the one for a term that appears in two documents far apart?
blocks.reveal: **the**. It occurs in almost every document, so nearly all its gaps are 1 and each fits in a single byte. A rare term's gaps are about as large as the docIDs themselves, so gap encoding saves almost nothing on it, though such lists are short anyway.

blocks.md: How much does this save on real postings? We encoded the docID lists of the Cranfield index (1,400 abstracts, 94,782 postings, terms from Lucene's EnglishAnalyzer) three ways. Fixed 32-bit docIDs take 379,128 bytes. Gaps plus VB take 103,214 bytes, 1.09 bytes per posting, because most gaps fit in one byte. Gaps plus gamma codes take 80,842 bytes, 6.82 bits per posting.

blocks.title: Cranfield docID postings under three encodings

scenes.caption: Measured on the Cranfield index: gap coding with VB cuts the docID lists to 27% of fixed 32-bit integers, and bit-level gamma codes to 21%, at the cost of slower bit-by-bit decoding.

blocks.md:
Compression makes in-place updates awkward: a postings list is a contiguous, compressed run, and inserting into it means rewriting it. The textbook design for a changing collection keeps a large **main index** plus a small in-memory **auxiliary index** for new documents, searches both and merges results, records deletions in an invalidation bit vector, and merges the auxiliary index into the main one when it grows too large.

Lucene generalizes this into **segments**. Each segment is a complete, independent inverted index. New documents create new segments, existing segments are merged, and a search runs over all of them.

blocks.title: Where a Lucene segment keeps the inverted index

scenes.caption: The dictionary lives in .tim (term dictionary); .tip is a small index into it so a term lookup does not scan the whole file.
The term entry points into .doc: docIDs and frequencies, in the Lucene 9.9 format packed in blocks of 128 with skip data. Positions sit in .pos, read only for queries that need them.
Simplified: an index is many segments, each a complete inverted index. New documents go into new segments; background merges combine segments into larger ones.

blocks.md: Segments also explain **near-real-time search**. Lucene can write a new segment and open it for searching without a full commit to disk, which is much cheaper; Elasticsearch calls this a **refresh** and by default refreshes every second, on indices that have received a search in the last 30 seconds, so a new document becomes searchable within about a second. Deletes work like the textbook's invalidation bit vector: a deleted document stays in its segment but is marked as not live (the .liv file records which documents are live), searches skip it, and it is physically dropped when its segment is merged.

Lucene shipped TF-IDF as its default ranking for years. Its `ClassicSimilarity` uses $\mathrm{tf} = \sqrt{\mathrm{freq}}$, $\mathrm{idf} = 1 + \ln\frac{\mathrm{docCount}+1}{\mathrm{docFreq}+1}$ and a length norm of $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{numTerms}}$. Here freq is tf, docCount is N, docFreq is df, and numTerms is the length of the document's field (a part such as its title or body) in tokens, so long fields get smaller weights: a cheaper stand-in for cosine's division by vector length. The +1 terms keep idf positive and finite even for a term in every document. Lucene 6.0 switched the default to **BM25** (Best Matching 25, from the Okapi research system at City University London), which keeps idf but makes each extra repeat of a term add less than the one before (issue [LUCENE-6789](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/LUCENE-6789)); `ClassicSimilarity` remains available.

blocks.title: idf in the six-doc corpus: log10 vs Lucene classic

scenes.caption: Textbook idf log10(N/df): the term in every document gets exactly 0.
Lucene classic idf 1 + ln((N+1)/(df+1)): the gets 1.000, never 0, and the ratio between rare and common terms shrinks (keys/cache 1.69 vs 4.42).

Its output reproduces the numbers of lesson 7.

blocks.md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

Where to go next: BM25 scoring on this same index is the course *BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting*; measuring whether a ranking is good is *Search evaluation basics*; learned term weights on an inverted index are *Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE*; dense vectors and ANN indexes are *Vector search and ANN*; fusing the two is *Hybrid search*; feeding results to an LLM is *Retrieval-augmented generation*.

TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

blocks.question: Using variable byte encoding (7 payload bits per byte), how many bytes does the gap 300 take?
options: 1 byte
2 bytes
3 bytes
4 bytes
blocks.explain: One byte holds values up to 127; two bytes hold 14 payload bits, values up to 16,383. 300 = 2 x 128 + 44, so it is written as the bytes 2 and 44, with the continuation bit set on the second byte.

blocks.question: Why does Lucene add documents by writing new segments instead of inserting postings into existing lists?
options: Segments are needed to compute idf
Postings are compressed contiguous runs, so in-place insertion would mean rewriting them; append-only segments plus background merges avoid that
Each segment can only hold one field
Lucene cannot store more than 128 documents per segment
blocks.explain: Compressed, gap-encoded postings cannot absorb an insert cheaply. Writing a fresh small segment is fast, and merges later rewrite several segments into one larger, well-compressed segment. This is the same main plus auxiliary idea from the textbook, generalized to many segments. The 128 is the packed block size, not a segment limit.
